extracted.intended_audience: computer science and NLP researchers, and computational social scientists studying media bias detection
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic literature-review style rubric describing categories, methods, datasets, evaluation practices, and methodological trade-offs for computational media-bias detection research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of methodological category (tNLP / ML / graph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches for media bias detection are organized into traditional NLP (tNLP), machine-learning-based (tbML, ntbML, nNN), and graph-based models. The choice of category should be guided by the task, data, explainability needs and the structure of the data (e.g., networked interactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: tNLP: accessible and explainable, often used as baselines; tbML (transformers): state-of-the-art accuracy but risk overfitting with limited data; ntbML/nNN: useful baselines and dataset-evaluation; graph-based: appropriate when social/network structure is central (framing, echo chambers, stance). Select the category aligned to task/data and compare across categories when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tNLP methods as explainable baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: tNLP methods are commonly used as baselines because of their explainability and proven effectiveness, and are increasingly adopted by social scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include count-based and embedding-based tNLP baselines (e.g., LIWC, TF-IDF, lexicon methods). Use them to assess gains from more complex models and to provide interpretable analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count-based approaches for bias quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify words and n-grams using reference lexicons to measure linguistic characteristics and compare texts (e.g., LIWC, custom bias lexicons, TF-IDF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common for topical categorization and selection/coverage/statements detection. Report standard metrics (precision, recall, F1) but note that some custom lexicons can still produce low F1 (example: custom bias lexicon F1=0.31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding-based (sparse vs dense) tNLP techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sparse embeddings (TF-IDF style) or dense word embeddings to represent texts and analyze associations; dense embeddings are used to examine associations (WEAT-style tests) while sparse embeddings survey word occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sparse embeddings good for occurrence analysis; dense embeddings (Word2Vec, etc.) suited to measuring semantic proximity (e.g., WEAT) and analyzing implicit associations across corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine-tune transformer-based models on bias-specific datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretrained transformers (BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ALBERT, BART, T5, etc.) are typically fine-tuned on bias-specific datasets and evaluated versus tNLP baselines (commonly via F1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create/select bias-specific datasets for fine-tuning. When reporting results, compare to strong tNLP baselines and alternative transformer variants to justify improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for transformer overfitting with limited data
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformers capture cross-domain dependencies but can over-fit in case of limited training data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If training data are limited, prefer simpler models, strong regularization, data augmentation, domain/task adaptation, or use tNLP baselines to check for overfitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate wider context (neighboring sentences, full article, event context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Including neighboring sentences, the full article, articles on the same event, or domain context improves detection of informational and framing bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models that incorporate event/context information (multi-sentence, cross-article or domain context) perform better for informational- and framing-bias detection (cf. RoBERTa context-inclusive models). Consider multi-document or context-aware encodings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multimodal and metadata features for political stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating audio, video, subtitles, and metadata alongside text can improve political stance detection and related bias classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimodal systems (text + audio/video + metadata) have yielded higher accuracy than text-only models for some stance tasks; include openSMILE or similar audio feature extractors where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipeline for automated debiasing: detect → recognize → mask → rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: Debiasing pipelines may consist of detection (identify biased tokens), recognition, masking, and generating less-biased rewrites (e.g., detect biased words with BERT, rewrite with BART).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paired corpora or edit histories to train detection and neutralization stages. Evaluate both detection quality and quality/faithfulness of generated debiased outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target-dependent sentiment and target information importance
rubrics_metrics.description: For sentiment-related tasks used as proxies for bias/stance, incorporating target information (i.e., aspect/target-aware classification) is crucial for transformer performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aspect-level or target-dependent sentiment classifiers (TSC). Incorporate external knowledge if necessary to improve target resolution and sentiment attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics and comparability caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Common evaluation metrics include precision, recall, and F1. However, many approaches use different datasets and tasks, making raw performance scores often incomparable across studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report precision/recall/F1, but also describe datasets, splits, and baselines. When cross-study comparison is infeasible, summarize methodological strengths and promising approaches rather than relying solely on numeric comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset construction and metadata best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets should include comprehensive metadata (task, label types, sizes, availability, link) and, when possible, annotator background; currently only 2 of 123 datasets report annotator background and dataset sizes are often small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide annotator demographics/background, dataset statistics, clear task definitions, and public access links. Prefer larger datasets (>30k annotations) or combining multiple datasets to improve robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize selection bias via dataset splits and bias probes
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating datasets, minimize selection bias by using clean non-overlapping site and date splits and include simple-model probes to detect dataset difficulty or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a site/date split to avoid leakage from outlet-specific language; include simple classifiers as difficulty/bias probes to reveal dataset artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data augmentation and pseudo-labeling to increase training data
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo-labeling, overlap-checking, meta-learning and other augmentation strategies can generate additional training data and improve classifiers where labeled data are scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply pseudo-labeling carefully (e.g., overlap-checking to avoid noise). Evaluate whether augmentation improves downstream performance and robustness versus introducing label noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove outlet-specific language effects in political stance models
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlet-specific language characteristics can leak political stance; methods like adversarial adaptation and triplet-loss pre-training can reduce outlet-specific signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate adversarial training or representation learning to remove publication-specific markers and train models that generalize across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-based exploitation of social/network structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When social-network structure matters (agenda-setting, framing, echo chambers, stance), employ graph-based models (graph NNs, graph auto-encoders, contrastive learning, label propagation) to encode multi-level context (sentence neighborhood, article, event).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community detection for echo-chamber analysis, node embeddings (node2vec), spectral graph transducers, and semi-supervised graph label propagation where labels are sparse. Combine graph features with textual encoders for best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-based classifiers: include bias lexicons and linguistic markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional non-neural classifiers benefit from hand-crafted features such as bias lexicons, sentiment scores, boosters, attitude markers, complexity and morality labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feature ablation to show feature importance. Feature-based baselines (LDA, LR, SVM, XGBoost) remain useful for dataset evaluation and explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze and mitigate bias in word embeddings and language models
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect bias in embeddings and LMs via association tests (e.g., WEAT), datasets like StereoSet, causal mediation analysis, and layer-wise inspection; mitigation strategies include synonym replacement, controlled generation, reinforcement-learning-based fine-tuning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report diagnostic tests (WEAT scores, StereoSet results), locate bias at component/layer level if possible, and evaluate mitigation impact on both bias metrics and utility/fluency of models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rationale/explainability labels to improve classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotator-provided rationale labels (highlighted bias-inducing words) improve model training and bias-classification performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect rationale annotations alongside labels when possible and evaluate models trained with and without rationale supervision to quantify improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hierarchical models and topic modeling to improve hyperpartisanship detection
rubrics_metrics.description: For document-level tasks such as hyperpartisanship, hierarchical architectures and inclusion of topic models (e.g., LDA) often improve performance over flat models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hierarchical attention networks combined with topic distributions. Empirical studies suggest hierarchical models with LDA outperform non-hierarchical variants in many setups.
